q-163208.name: Question 1
q-163208.problem:
Consider the function $f(x,y)$ and the region $D$ given by

$$
f(x,y)=3y-2x,\,D=\{(x,y)\,:\,0\le x\le y,\,0\le y\le 3\}.
$$

According to the mean value theorem for double integrals, there exists a point $(a,b)\in D$ such that the volume of the solid enclosed between the surface $z=f(x,y)$ and the $xy$-plane over the region $D$ equals the volume of the right cylinder with base $D$ and height $f(a,b).$ Find $b$ given that $a=1.$
q-163208.worked_solution:
According to the mean value theorem for double integrals, there exists a point $(a,b)\in D$ such that

$$
{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\,\text{d}A=f(a,b)\cdot \text{Area}(D).
$$

Evaluating the integral on the left-hand side, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{D}(3y-2x)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3}{\int }_{0}^{y}(3y-2x)\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3}[3xy-{x}^{2}]_{x=0}^{x=y}\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3}2{y}^{2}\,\text{d}y \\  & ={[\frac{2{y}^{3}}{3}]}_{y=0}^{y=3} \\  & =18.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Area}(D) & ={∬}_{D}\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3}{\int }_{0}^{y}\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3}[x]_{x=0}^{x=y}\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3}y\,\text{d}y \\  & ={[\frac{{y}^{2}}{2}]}_{y=0}^{y=3} \\  & =\frac{9}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Also, we are told that $a=1.$ So, our initial equation simplifies to

$$
\begin{aligned}18 & =f(1,b)\cdot \frac{9}{2} \\ 18 & =(3b-2\cdot 1)\cdot \frac{9}{2} \\ 4 & =3b-2 \\ 6 & =3b \\ b & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that $(1,2)\in D.$ Therefore, the answer is $b=2.$

q-163151.problem:
Consider the function $f(x,y)$ and the region $D$ given by

$$
f(x,y)=2x+{y}^{2},\,D=\{(x,y)\,:\,0\le x\le 2,\,0\le y\le 3\}.

$$
\text{Area}(D)=2\cdot 3=6.

q-163197.name: Question 3
q-163197.problem:
Consider the function $f(x,y)$ and the region $D$ given by

$$
f(x,y)=2xy,\,D=\{(x,y)\,:\,0\le x\le \frac{y}{2},\,0\le y\le 4\}.
$$

According to the mean value theorem for double integrals, there exists a point $(a,b)\in D$ such that the volume of the solid enclosed between the surface $z=f(x,y)$ and the $xy$-plane over the region $D$ equals the volume of the right cylinder with base $D$ and height $f(a,b).$ Find $a$ given that $b=3.$
q-163197.worked_solution:
According to the mean value theorem for double integrals, there exists a point $(a,b)\in D$ such that

$$
{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\,\text{d}A=f(a,b)\cdot \text{Area}(D).
$$

Evaluating the integral on the left-hand side, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{D}2xy\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{4}{\int }_{0}^{y/2}2xy\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{4}[{x}^{2}y]_{x=0}^{x=y/2}\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{4}\frac{{y}^{3}}{4}\,\text{d}y \\  & =[\frac{{y}^{4}}{16}]_{y=0}^{y=4} \\  & =16.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Area}(D) & ={∬}_{D}\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{4}{\int }_{0}^{y/2}\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{4}[x]_{x=0}^{x=y/2}\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{4}\frac{y}{2}\,\text{d}y \\  & ={[\frac{{y}^{2}}{4}]}_{y=0}^{y=4} \\  & =4.\end{aligned}
$$

Also, we are told that $b=3.$ So, our initial equation simplifies to

$$
\begin{aligned}16 & =f(a,3)\cdot 4 \\ 16 & =(2a\cdot 3)\cdot 4 \\ 16 & =24a \\ a & =\frac{2}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that $(\frac{2}{3},3)\in D.$ Therefore, the answer is $a=\frac{2}{3}.$

q-163205.name: Question 5
q-163205.problem:
Consider the function $f(x,y)$ and the region $D$ given by

$$
f(x,y)=2x+y,\,D=\{(x,y)\,:\,\frac{y}{2}\le x\le y,\,\,0\le y\le 6\}.
$$

According to the mean value theorem for double integrals, there exists a point $(a,b)\in D$ such that the volume of the solid enclosed between the surface $z=f(x,y)$ and the $xy$-plane over the region $D$ equals the volume of the right cylinder with base $D$ and height $f(a,b).$ Find $a$ given that $b=4.$
q-163205.worked_solution:
According to the mean value theorem for double integrals, there exists a point $(a,b)\in D$ such that

$$
{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\,\text{d}A=f(a,b)\cdot \text{Area}(D).
$$

Evaluating the integral on the left-hand side, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{D}(2x+y)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{6}{\int }_{y/2}^{y}(2x+y)\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{6}[{x}^{2}+xy]_{x=y/2}^{x=y}\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{6}([{y}^{2}+{y}^{2}]-[\frac{{y}^{2}}{4}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{2}])\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{6}\frac{5{y}^{2}}{4}\,\text{d}y \\  & ={[\frac{5{y}^{3}}{12}]}_{y=0}^{y=6} \\  & =90.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Area}(D) & ={∬}_{D}\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{6}{\int }_{y/2}^{y}\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{6}[x]_{x=y/2}^{x=y}\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{6}\frac{y}{2}\,\text{d}y \\  & ={[\frac{{y}^{2}}{4}]}_{y=0}^{y=6} \\  & =9.\end{aligned}
$$

Also, we are told that $b=4.$ So, our initial equation simplifies to

$$
\begin{aligned}90 & =f(a,4)\cdot 9 \\ 90 & =(2a+4)\cdot 9 \\ 10 & =2a+4 \\ 6 & =2a \\ a & =3.\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that $(3,4)\in D.$ Therefore, the answer is $a=3.$

q-163257.name: Question 11
q-163257.problem: Find the average value of the function $f(x,y)={y}^{2}$ on the disk of radius $2$ centered at the origin.
q-163257.worked_solution:
First, notice that 

$$
\text{Area}(D)=\pi \cdot {2}^{2}=4\pi .
$$

The average value of the function over a region $D$ is given by

$$
{f}_{\text{ave}}=\frac{1}{\text{Area}(D)}\,{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\,\text{d}A.
$$

We will use the change of variables formula in the form

$$
{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\text{ }dA={∬}_{Δ}\text{ }f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,r\text{ }drd\theta .
$$

In polar coordinates $(r,\theta ),$ the region can be expressed as 

$$
Δ=\{(r,\theta )\,:\,0\le r\le 2,\,0\le \theta <2\pi \}.
$$

Using the change of variables formula, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}{y}^{2}\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{Δ}(r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )^{2}\,r\,\text{d}r\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{\int }_{0}^{2}{r}^{3}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta \,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{sin}^{2}⁡\theta {\int }_{0}^{2}{r}^{3}\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{sin}^{2}⁡\theta \,{[\frac{{r}^{4}}{4}]}_{0}^{2}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{sin}^{2}⁡\theta (4-0)\text{d}\theta  \\  & =4{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{sin}^{2}⁡\theta \,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =4{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\frac{1}{2}(1-\operatorname{cos}⁡2\theta )\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =2{[\theta -\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta ]}_{0}^{2\pi } \\  & =2[(2\pi -0)-\frac{1}{2}(\operatorname{sin}⁡4\pi -\operatorname{sin}⁡0)] \\  & =2\cdot 2\pi  \\  & =4\pi .\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, 

$$
{f}_{\text{ave}}=\frac{1}{4\pi }\cdot 4\pi =1.
$$

q-163256.name: Question 12
q-163256.problem: Find the average value of the function $f(x,y)={e}^{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}$ on the disk of radius $\frac{1}{2}$ centered at the origin.
q-163256.worked_solution:
First, notice that 

$$
\text{Area}(D)=\pi \cdot {(\frac{1}{2})}^{2}=\frac{\pi }{4}.
$$

The average value of the function over a region $D$ is given by

$$
{f}_{\text{ave}}=\frac{1}{\text{Area}(D)}\,{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\,\text{d}A.
$$

We will use the change of variables formula in the form

$$
{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\text{ }dA={∬}_{Δ}\text{ }f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,r\text{ }drd\theta .
$$

In polar coordinates $(r,\theta ),$ the region can be expressed as 

$$
Δ=\{(r,\theta )\,:\,0\le r\le \frac{1}{2},\,0\le \theta <2\pi \}.
$$

Using the change of variables formula, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}{e}^{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{Δ}{e}^{(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{2}+(r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )^{2}}\,r\,\text{d}r\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={∬}_{Δ}{e}^{{r}^{2}}\,r\,\text{d}r\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\,{[\frac{{e}^{{r}^{2}}}{2}]}_{0}^{1/2}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }(\frac{{e}^{1/4}}{2}-\frac{1}{2})\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{\sqrt[4]{e}-1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{\sqrt[4]{e}-1}{2}[\theta ]_{0}^{2\pi } \\  & =\frac{\sqrt[4]{e}-1}{2}(2\pi -0) \\  & =(\sqrt[4]{e}-1)\pi .\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, 

$$
{f}_{\text{ave}}=\frac{4}{\pi }\cdot (\sqrt[4]{e}-1)\pi =4(\sqrt[4]{e}-1).
$$

q-163277.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14157768/assets/06a853735916ae3219eea02fa7e7e30d9e941106600cd5b642d951f553aace59.png)

Find the average value of the function $f(x,y)=5y({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})$ on the semicircle shown above.
q-163277.worked_solution:
First, notice that 

$$
\text{Area}(D)=\frac{1}{2}\cdot \pi \cdot {1}^{2}=\frac{\pi }{2}.
$$

The average value of the function over a region $D$ is given by

$$
{f}_{\text{ave}}=\frac{1}{\text{Area}(D)}\,{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\,\text{d}A.
$$

We will use the change of variables formula in the form

$$
{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\text{ }dA={∬}_{Δ}\text{ }f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,r\text{ }drd\theta .
$$

Notice that the region $D$ represents a portion of the disk of radius $1$ centered at 
$(1,0).$

Cartesian and polar coordinates are connected by the following equations:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}x=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\ y=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \end{aligned}
$$

With that is mind, let's now write the $y=-\sqrt{2x-{x}^{2}}$ in polar coordinates:

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =-\sqrt{2x-{x}^{2}} \\ {y}^{2} & =2x-{x}^{2} \\ {x}^{2}+{y}^{2} & =2x \\ (r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{2}+(r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )^{2} & =2r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\ {r}^{2}({cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta ) & =2r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\ {r}^{2} & =2r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\ {r}^{2}-2r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & =0 \\ r(r-2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

 

Since $r$ cannot be identical to zero on the entire semicircle, we must have $r=2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta .$

Therefore, in polar coordinates $(r,\theta ),$ the region can be expressed as 

$$
Δ=\{(r,\theta )\,:\,0\le r\le 2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,-\frac{\pi }{2}\le \theta \le 0\}.
$$

Therefore, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}5y({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{Δ}5r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ((r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{2}+(r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )^{2})\,r\,\text{d}r\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi /2}^{0}{\int }_{0}^{2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }5{r}^{4}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ({cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi /2}^{0}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta {\int }_{0}^{2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }5{r}^{4}\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi /2}^{0}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta [{r}^{5}]_{0}^{2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi /2}^{0}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ((2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{5}-0)\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =32{\int }_{-\pi /2}^{0}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta {cos}^{5}⁡\theta \,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =32{[-\frac{1}{6}{cos}^{6}⁡\theta ]}_{-\pi /2}^{0} \\  & =-\frac{16}{3}[{cos}^{6}⁡(0)-{cos}^{6}⁡(-\frac{\pi }{2})] \\  & =-\frac{16}{3}(1-0) \\  & =-\frac{16}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, 

$$
{f}_{\text{ave}}=\frac{1}{(\frac{\pi }{2})}\cdot (-\frac{16}{3})=-\frac{32}{3\pi }.
$$

q-163068.name: Question 14
q-163068.problem: Find the average value of the function $f(x,y)=2x+y$ on the portion of the disk of radius $2$ centered at the origin, where $y\ge 0.$
q-163068.worked_solution:
First, let's sketch our region $D:$ 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14157768/assets/b5ba69ab02aa13e201b7b9113f6a36e705ad19e6412499504afc4f239459a8f3.png)

Notice that 

$$
\text{Area}(D)=\frac{1}{2}\cdot \pi \cdot {2}^{2}=2\pi .
$$

The average value of the function over a region $D$ is given by

$$
{f}_{\text{ave}}=\frac{1}{\text{Area}(D)}\,{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\,\text{d}A.
$$

We will use the change of variables formula in the form

$$
{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\text{ }dA={∬}_{Δ}\text{ }f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,r\text{ }drd\theta .
$$

In polar coordinates $(r,\theta ),$ the region can be expressed as 

$$
Δ=\{(r,\theta )\,:\,0\le r\le 2,\,0\le \theta \le \pi \}.
$$

Using the change of variables formula, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}(2x+y)\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{Δ}(2r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,r\,\text{d}r\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }{\int }_{0}^{2}{r}^{2}(2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }(2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ){\int }_{0}^{2}{r}^{2}\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }(2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,{[\frac{{r}^{3}}{3}]}_{0}^{2}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }(2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )(\frac{{2}^{3}}{3}-0)\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{8}{3}{\int }_{0}^{\pi }(2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{8}{3}[2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta -\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ]_{0}^{\pi } \\  & =\frac{8}{3}((2\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi )-\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi ))-(2\operatorname{sin}⁡(0)-\operatorname{cos}⁡(0))) \\  & =\frac{8}{3}(1+1) \\  & =\frac{16}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, 

$$
{f}_{\text{ave}}=\frac{1}{2\pi }\cdot \frac{16}{3}=\frac{8}{3\pi }.
$$

q-163260.name: Question 15
q-163260.problem: Find the average value of the function $f(x,y)=\frac{2}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+1}$ on the portion of the disk of radius $3$ centered at the origin, where $x\le 0.$
q-163260.worked_solution:
First, let's sketch our region $D:$ 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14157768/assets/25c1f00e588ddaa130f854d9f4e9dfe9b1158d7952a01bae8108ea4b94d3c347.png)

Notice that 

$$
\text{Area}(D)=\frac{1}{2}\cdot \pi \cdot {3}^{2}=\frac{9\pi }{2}.
$$

The average value of the function over a region $D$ is given by

$$
{f}_{\text{ave}}=\frac{1}{\text{Area}(D)}\,{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\,\text{d}A.
$$

We will use the change of variables formula in the form

$$
{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\text{ }dA={∬}_{Δ}\text{ }f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,r\text{ }drd\theta .
$$

In polar coordinates $(r,\theta ),$ the region can be expressed as 

$$
Δ=\{(r,\theta )\,:\,0\le r\le 3,\,\frac{\pi }{2}\le \theta \le \frac{3\pi }{2}\}.
$$

Using the change of variables formula, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}\frac{2}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+1}\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{Δ}\frac{2}{(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{2}+(r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )^{2}+1}\,r\,\text{d}r\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /2}^{3\pi /2}{\int }_{0}^{3}\frac{2r}{{r}^{2}+1}\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /2}^{3\pi /2}[\operatorname{ln}⁡({r}^{2}+1)]_{0}^{3}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /2}^{3\pi /2}(\operatorname{ln}⁡10-\operatorname{ln}⁡1)\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡10{\int }_{\pi /2}^{3\pi /2}\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡10[\theta ]_{\pi /2}^{3\pi /2} \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡10(\frac{3\pi }{2}-\frac{\pi }{2}) \\  & =\pi \operatorname{ln}⁡10.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, 

$$
{f}_{\text{ave}}=\frac{2}{9\pi }\cdot \pi \operatorname{ln}⁡10=\frac{2\operatorname{ln}⁡10}{9}.
$$

Find the average value of the function f(x,y)=2x2+y2+1 on the portion of the disk of radius 3 centered at the origin, where x≤0.

a
2ln⁡109
b
ln⁡109
c
2ln⁡103
d
4ln⁡29
e
4ln⁡103
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

First, let's sketch our region D:

Notice that

Area(D)=12⋅π⋅32=9π2.

The average value of the function over a region D is given by

fave=1Area(D)∬Df(x,y)dA.

We will use the change of variables formula in the form

∬Df(x,y) dA=∬Δ f(rcos⁡θ,rsin⁡θ)r drdθ.

In polar coordinates (r,θ), the region can be expressed as

Δ={(r,θ):0≤r≤3,π2≤θ≤3π2}.

Using the change of variables formula, we obtain

∬D2x2+y2+1dA=∬Δ2(rcos⁡θ)2+(rsin⁡θ)2+1rdrdθ=∫π/23π/2∫032rr2+1drdθ=∫π/23π/2[ln⁡(r2+1)]03dθ=∫π/23π/2(ln⁡10−ln⁡1)dθ=ln⁡10∫π/23π/2dθ=ln⁡10[θ]π/23π/2=ln⁡10(3π2−π2)=πln⁡10.

Therefore,

fave=29π⋅πln⁡10=2ln⁡109.
